en: There was Kokand, looming dark.
It was Kokand itself.
The orphan boy grew excited;
He had reached Kokand.
These were my mother's words:
'If you can, by Kokand,
My only one, pass without approaching,' she said.
The reason not to approach was this:
When my holy father lived,
He used to humiliate Kokand,
Six thousand silver ingots and a thousand otter pelts
He used to take in tribute.
If they did not pay that tribute,
If they would not obey his words,
My father did as he pleased.
Loading elephants, taking gold coins,
If his anger once took hold,
He took a thousand dark-eyed people.
When he wrought havoc among the Sarts,
He plundered their valuables.
He truly wrought destruction;
Unable to endure that suffering,
Many of them were left weeping.
These were my mother's words:
'The high official in Kokand
Has a grudge against your father Khan Manas;
He will be hostile toward you,' she said.
'He will be less inclined to reconciliation,' she said.
“When I go to the khan of Kokand,
Let me not fall needlessly into disaster.
In a Sart's house in Kokand,
There is grain beer kept in a leather bucket.
If he serves food while singing his song,
There is burning poison mixed in.
There is grain beer brewed from millet,
With a weakening poison mixed inside.
In the khan of Kokand's palace,
Beneath a gold-patterned carpet,
Dug underneath,
There is a pit forty cubits deep.
If I do not make sport now,
The yellow water from his heart—
If I do not draw it all out,
Going ahead first to Kokand,
If I do not cause a rout,
Their households are loaded on donkeys;
Later they will show it,
These Sarts have a grudge.
Rather than fear this Kokand,
Rather than turn back without meeting him,
Rather than retreat afraid before meeting him,
Let me sink away without being born;
Let me die before my appointed death.
The khan of Kokand's cruelty,
If he rises against me, let me see it.
Rather than go in fear of Kokand,
Let me sink away without being born.
Let me meet the khan of Kokand,
And pass after greeting him.
If Kokand grows insolent,
Let me bring it to its end altogether.
Rather than go in fear of this Kokand,
Let me depart while young.
Where he steps is like a ridge;
Of the high official, Semetey
Would not be said to have fled in fear.
My life is a sacrifice to my honor.
High official of Kokand!
While my dear life remains,
Let me meet him once!”
The orphan servant born of Manas,
In the blink of an eye,
Before one could say a word,
Taking cover in its narrow streets,
Passing through spacious Kokand,
Driven to frenzy by his courage,
The high official of Kokand's
Guard he encountered.
Majestic, the orphan cared nothing;
The high official of Kokand
He valued less than a trouser hem.
Courage and lion-hearted valor,
To Manas's orphan son,
Had been given without measure.
The high official's wrestler
He valued less than a trouser hem.
The mount beneath him
Was Khan Temir's Aktulpar;
What he held in his hand
Was Ismayyl's steel blade.
That unruly orphan himself
Had resourcefulness beyond other people.
He had brought from Bukhara
Khan Koloy's spear.
What he wore upon him,
With a golden collar and copper sleeves,
Double mail with lark-eye rings,
A gold-thread collar and broad jacket,
Impenetrable to bullets when worn in battle,
Was the white coat Kanykey had made.
Showing her motherly care,
To the only one left by the valiant hero
She had given it to wear as a gift.
The gray pouch-belt at his waist,
Proven when girded on,
Was that poor one's inheritance from Manas.
When he cried out and bound it at his waist,
The White Ishan became his companion.
When he shouted and bound it at his waist,
The forty chiltens became his companions.
Those who knew would say:
“God brought it to the generous hero;
It appeared from the unseen world,
Was found in the desolate desert—
The pouch-belt that fell from heaven.”
Those who did not know said this:
“Six Cities, Kokand’s
Andijan—when he ravaged them,
From a white-turbaned holy man,
From a mullah in a motley coat,
He seized that pouch-belt,” they said.
Girding on the gray pouch-belt,
Your unruly boy born of Khan Manas,
Wrathful and grim,
Drew the attention of all who saw him.
With the ancestral spirit upon him, towering,
He looked like your generous Manas himself.
Taking cover in the narrow streets,
Passing through Great Kokand,
He went to the high official.
The high official's sentry,
Standing and looking at the boy,
Shouted and ran on foot.
His wrestler, flustered,
Before the high official
Spoke ill of Semetey:
“My lord khan, hear my words!
Do you know what I know?
Have you sensed what I sensed?
My lord, have you seen what I saw?
That scoundrel has arrived.
My lord, that wretch has arrived.
The one who started the turmoil,
One arm of our Camel Wrestler
He tore clean off.
To Khan Temir's city
He wandered and grew up;
That blood-drinker has arrived.
He has reached twelve years old.
He will not let a plow turn.
May good fortune forsake me if I lie!
He will not let us remain in this Kokand.
If we do not seize him now,
If we do not cut short that only child's life,
If we do not put him out like a fire,
The orphan will bring us torment.
'Tribute left by my father,' he will say;
'A token left by Manas,' he will say.
Six thousand silver ingots, a thousand otter pelts,
Renewing that tribute,
He will bring us torment;
He will take his revenge far and wide!
That wretched orphan, the image of blood-stained Manas,
Dragging along the road
Whoever talks back,
He will have the Dangyts tear them apart.
Thus he will slaughter Kokand.
If we do not find a way now,
If we do not cut off his head now,
God damn that orphan!
Of this Kokand here,
He will slaughter them without leaving one!”
The high official in Kokand,
After hearing this,
Revealed his dreadful purpose,
And gave orders to his wrestlers.
From marksmen who never missed,
“Capture Semetey and bring him,” he said,
And sent ten of them.
From skilled spearmen,
From strong men who knew the enemy's tricks,
He sent ten of them.
From warriors who wielded iron-headed maces,
He sent ten of them.
From mighty swordsmen,
He sent ten of them.
When a fearsome gun cracked,
From strong men who did not flinch,
He sent ten of them.
When a black gun boomed,
From strong men who would not flee,
He sent ten of them.
Having heard it, the high official
Worked himself into a terrible fury.
Shouting, calling them scoundrels,
He raged at his wrestlers.
“Capture Semetey and bring him;
Capture the orphan and bring him,
Deliver him straight into my hands.
If you do not obey my words—
My wrestlers, all of you listen!
To capture Semetey,
To seize the orphan,
To put him to death,
To kill him and take his head,
To avenge the Camel Wrestler,
The prince's orphan son,
To bring disaster upon him!”
Saying this, the high official
Beat the drum.
When they heard this news,
His wrestlers hurried in confusion.
The accursed fellows who had received orders
“To capture Semetey,”
Their spears bristling,
Their battle-axes showing,
Drawing the attention of onlookers,
Their leaders spreading their arms,
His wrestlers rushed upon the boy,
Swarming forward with limbs flailing.
Then the boy Semetey,
Offspring of the lion protected by Kyzyr,
The orphan rode without looking back,
Paying no heed to Kokand,
Caring not a straw for death.
His eyes blazed like fire.
His splendid teeth, like gates,
That offspring of a prince
Chewed hard, over and over.
His father, fierce Manas,
Your orphan was born to surpass.
With Aktulpar, heedless,
The wrestlers who rushed upon him
He valued less than his shin.
Did you see his dauntless nature?
The boy went on, heedless.
He did not look up or down,
The offspring of that accursed one,
Did not think he would die.
The leopard who poured blood into dark waters—
He was that leopard's offspring;
The fierce hero who burned grassy lands—
He was that hero's offspring.
From his father back to his forefathers,
They spared none who grappled with them,
Drank blood and were never sated,
Had their undertakings favored by God,
And never went back on their word.
Perhaps you have heard of him,
Khan Manas's only son.
Before this, the boy Semetey
Had never known such enemies;
The generous hero's only son
Had never charged into battle with a shout.
